notes: Set-wide: Hindu tradition is many traditions. Lessons say 'many Hindus', 'the story says', 'in the Bhagavata Purana', and grownups.source names where family or regional tellings differ from the Sanskrit texts.

Gentlest tellings throughout: Ravana and the war in Lanka are named only as 'the long trouble in Lanka'; Narasimha is left out of Prahlad's story; Holika's fate is not described (her trick fails); Indra's thunderbolt in the baby Hanuman story becomes 'stopped him'; Kaliya is tired, not wounded. A Keeper should confirm these softenings are acceptable to families.

Spellings: Ganesha, Hanuman, Rama, Krishna, Sita, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Prahlad, Yashoda are the same in English and Spanish (unaccented, as in English). Kevat follows the Hindi spelling (Kewat is also common).
Devanagari is used only in 'means' for words whose spelling is standard: गणेश, हनुमान, होली, गंगा, लक्ष्मी, यमुना, राखी, सरस्वती, नमस्ते. Please confirm.

Some dialogue is given to Shiva, Parvati, Krishna, Rama, Vyasa and Uddalaka in short paraphrased lines; none of it is a quotation of a translation. A Keeper may prefer fewer invented lines for deities.

Several stories are popular tellings with no single Sanskrit source (the mango race, Holika's shawl, Shabari's tasted berries, the squirrel, the broken tusk as pen, Krishna and Draupadi's sari strip, the silent world before Saraswati, Kevat's 'both boatmen' line). Each is flagged as such in grownups.source and notes.

en.title: Ganesha and the race around the world
en.means: गणेश: the elephant-headed god of new beginnings

story.head: a mango for the winner
story.text: On the mountain Kailash, Shiva and Parvati had two sons. Kartikeya was quick and strong. Ganesha had an elephant's head and a big, kind heart. One day a sage brought them a single golden mango, and both boys wanted it.

story.head: a race around the world
story.text: Shiva smiled. “Whoever goes all the way around the world first,” he said, “wins the mango.” Kartikeya jumped onto his peacock and zoomed into the sky, over oceans and forests and snowy hills.

story.head: Ganesha walks around his parents
story.text: Ganesha's ride was a little mouse, not very fast at all. So Ganesha sat and thought. Then he stood up, folded his hands, and walked slowly all the way around his mother and father, and bowed.

story.head: my whole world
story.text: “Why did you walk around us?” asked Parvati. “Because you two are my whole world,” said Ganesha. His parents laughed with joy and gave him the mango. Kartikeya landed later, windblown and tired, and found his brother already smiling.

game.prompt: who did what? tap the pairs.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like Ganesha taking one careful step, and breathe out slowly, like the next step. four slow steps around the people you love.
en.carry: my family is my whole world

grownups.source: a well-loved family telling. In the Shiva Purana the prize is the chance to marry first; in many South Indian tellings it is a mango, and Kartikeya goes off to Palani hill. Families tell it many ways.
grownups.ask: who are the people who make up your whole world?

es.title: Ganesha y la carrera alrededor del mundo
es.means: गणेश: el dios con cabeza de elefante de los nuevos comienzos

story.head: un mango para el ganador
story.text: En la montaña Kailash, Shiva y Parvati tenían dos hijos. Kartikeya era rápido y fuerte. Ganesha tenía cabeza de elefante y un corazón grande y bueno. Un día un sabio les trajo un solo mango dorado, y los dos lo querían.

story.head: una carrera alrededor del mundo
story.text: Shiva sonrió. “Quien dé primero la vuelta a todo el mundo”, dijo, “se gana el mango”. Kartikeya saltó sobre su pavo real y salió volando por el cielo, sobre mares, bosques y montes nevados.

story.head: Ganesha rodea a sus padres
story.text: Ganesha montaba un ratoncito que no era nada rápido. Así que Ganesha se sentó a pensar. Luego se levantó, juntó las manos, caminó despacio alrededor de su mamá y su papá, y les hizo una reverencia.

story.head: todo mi mundo
story.text: “¿Por qué caminaste a nuestro alrededor?”, preguntó Parvati. “Porque ustedes dos son todo mi mundo”, dijo Ganesha. Sus padres rieron de alegría y le dieron el mango. Kartikeya llegó después, cansado y despeinado, y encontró a su hermano sonriendo.

game.prompt: ¿quién hizo qué? toca las parejas.

es.breath: inhala despacio, como Ganesha dando un paso con cuidado, y exhala despacio, como el siguiente paso. cuatro pasos lentos alrededor de quienes quieres.
es.carry: mi familia es todo mi mundo

grownups.source: un relato familiar muy querido. En el Shiva Purana el premio es casarse primero; en muchos relatos del sur de la India es un mango, y Kartikeya se va a la colina de Palani. Las familias lo cuentan de muchas maneras.
grownups.ask: ¿quiénes son las personas que forman todo tu mundo?

sources.ref: Rudra Samhita, Kumara Khanda (the brothers' race)

sources.work: South Indian temple and family tradition (Palani)

notes: for the Keeper: the Shiva Purana version is a race to decide who marries first (Ganesha marries Siddhi and Buddhi); the mango comes from Tamil tellings where Narada brings the fruit and Kartikeya, upset, leaves for Palani. I used the mango and a happy ending without Kartikeya's departure; grownups.source mentions Palani. Chapter numbers in the Kumara Khanda not cited because I am not certain of them.
for the Keeper: 'a sage' is left unnamed (Narada in Tamil tellings). Some tellings have Ganesha circle his parents a set number of times; I gave no count.

en.title: Hanuman's leap across the sea
en.means: हनुमान: Rama's brave and loyal monkey friend

story.head: Sita is far away
story.text: Rama's wife Sita had been carried far away to the island of Lanka, across the wide, wide sea. Rama's monkey friends sat on the shore, worried. Nobody could jump that far. Nobody, they thought.

story.head: a reminder from Jambavan
story.text: Wise old Jambavan, the bear, turned to Hanuman. “You are the son of the wind,” he said. “You have forgotten how strong you are.” Hanuman remembered. He began to grow, bigger and bigger, as tall as a hill.

story.head: one huge leap
story.text: Hanuman climbed Mount Mahendra, pressed his feet down hard, and sprang into the sky. He flew over the waves like the wind itself, his tail streaming behind him, with Rama in his heart.

story.head: a mountain offers a rest
story.text: Halfway across, a mountain named Mainaka rose up out of the sea. “Rest on me a while,” it said. Hanuman touched it kindly, said thank you, and kept going. At last he landed in Lanka, ready to find Sita.

items: Jambavan reminded Hanuman how strong he was.
yes: wise Jambavan told him he had forgotten his own strength.
Hanuman crossed the sea on a raft of logs.
not in it: he leaped from Mount Mahendra and flew over the waves.
a mountain rose from the sea to offer him a rest.
yes: Mainaka rose up; Hanuman thanked it and kept going.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like Hanuman growing taller, and breathe out slowly, like his long flight over the waves. four slow breaths.
en.carry: I can do more than I think

grownups.source: Valmiki's Ramayana: Jambavan's reminder ends the Kishkindha Kanda, and the leap opens the Sundara Kanda. Tulsidas tells it again in the Ramcharitmanas, and many families read the Sundara Kanda on its own.
grownups.ask: when has someone reminded you that you could do something hard?

es.title: el gran salto de Hanuman sobre el mar
es.means: हनुमान: el valiente y fiel amigo mono de Rama

story.head: Sita está muy lejos
story.text: Sita, la esposa de Rama, había sido llevada muy lejos, a la isla de Lanka, al otro lado del ancho mar. Los amigos monos de Rama estaban sentados en la orilla, preocupados. Nadie podía saltar tan lejos. Nadie, pensaban.

story.head: Jambavan le recuerda algo
story.text: El sabio y viejo Jambavan, el oso, miró a Hanuman. “Eres hijo del viento”, le dijo. “Se te olvidó lo fuerte que eres”. Hanuman se acordó. Empezó a crecer, más y más grande, alto como una colina.

story.head: un salto enorme
story.text: Hanuman subió al monte Mahendra, apretó los pies contra el suelo y saltó al cielo. Voló sobre las olas como el mismo viento, con la cola ondeando detrás y Rama en el corazón.

story.head: una montaña le ofrece descanso
story.text: A mitad del camino, una montaña llamada Mainaka salió del mar. “Descansa en mí un rato”, le dijo. Hanuman la tocó con cariño, le dio las gracias y siguió. Por fin llegó a Lanka, listo para encontrar a Sita.

items: Jambavan le recordó a Hanuman lo fuerte que era.
sí: el sabio Jambavan le dijo que había olvidado su propia fuerza.
Hanuman cruzó el mar en una balsa de troncos.
no: saltó desde el monte Mahendra y voló sobre las olas.
una montaña salió del mar para ofrecerle descanso.
sí: Mainaka salió del agua; Hanuman le dio las gracias y siguió.

es.breath: inhala despacio, como Hanuman creciendo, y exhala despacio, como su largo vuelo sobre las olas. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: puedo hacer más de lo que creo

grownups.source: el Ramayana de Valmiki: el recordatorio de Jambavan cierra el Kishkindha Kanda y el salto abre el Sundara Kanda. Tulsidas lo vuelve a contar en el Ramcharitmanas, y muchas familias leen el Sundara Kanda por sí solo.
grownups.ask: ¿cuándo alguien te recordó que podías hacer algo difícil?

sources.ref: Kishkindha Kanda, final sargas (Jambavan's speech); Sundara Kanda, sarga 1 (the leap, Mainaka)

notes: for the Keeper: Sita's abduction by Ravana is told only as 'carried far away'; Ravana is not named. Surasa and Simhika, the other two meetings on the flight, are left out as too frightening for small children.
for the Keeper: 'with Rama in his heart' is a devotional touch, not a detail of Valmiki's text.

en.title: Prahlad and the bonfire of Holi
en.means: होली: the spring festival of colors and bonfires

story.head: a king who wanted all the praise
story.text: Long ago a proud king named Hiranyakashipu wanted everyone to worship him alone. But his own little son, Prahlad, loved Vishnu. Morning and night, Prahlad sang Vishnu's name, and he would not stop.

story.head: Prahlad keeps singing
story.text: The king tried and tried to change Prahlad's mind. Prahlad stayed gentle and polite, and he stayed just the same. “Vishnu is everywhere,” he said quietly, “even right here with me.”

story.head: Holika's magic shawl
story.text: The king's sister, Holika, had a magic shawl that fire could not burn. She had a plan. She would sit in a bonfire with Prahlad on her lap, wrapped safe inside her shawl.

story.head: the fire does not touch Prahlad
story.text: The fire was lit. Prahlad said Vishnu's name, calm and steady. A wind lifted the shawl off Holika and wrapped it around Prahlad. The flames could not touch him, and Holika's trick did not work. Prahlad walked out safe. Every year, the night before Holi, many Hindus light a bonfire to remember him.

game.prompt: who did what? tap the pairs.
pairs: had a shawl fire couldn't burn
is lit the night before Holi

en.breath: breathe in slowly, calm and steady like Prahlad, and breathe out slowly, like the cool wind that carried the shawl. four slow breaths.
en.carry: I can stay kind and still be myself

grownups.source: the Bhagavata Purana (book 7) tells of Prahlad's love for Vishnu. The bonfire and Holika come from later tellings and from Holika Dahan, the bonfire night before Holi. In some tellings Holika's protection is a blessing, not a shawl.
grownups.ask: when is it hard to stay gentle and still be yourself?

es.title: Prahlad y la fogata de Holi
es.means: होली: la fiesta de primavera de los colores y las fogatas

story.head: un rey que quería todas las alabanzas
story.text: Hace mucho tiempo, un rey orgulloso llamado Hiranyakashipu quería que todos lo adoraran solo a él. Pero su propio hijito, Prahlad, amaba a Vishnu. Mañana y noche, Prahlad cantaba el nombre de Vishnu, y no dejaba de hacerlo.

story.head: Prahlad sigue cantando
story.text: El rey intentó una y otra vez que Prahlad cambiara de idea. Prahlad seguía amable y educado, y seguía igual. “Vishnu está en todas partes”, decía en voz baja, “incluso aquí conmigo”.

story.head: el chal mágico de Holika
story.text: Holika, la hermana del rey, tenía un chal mágico que el fuego no podía quemar. Tenía un plan. Se sentaría en una fogata con Prahlad en el regazo, bien envuelta en su chal.

story.head: el fuego no toca a Prahlad
story.text: Encendieron el fuego. Prahlad dijo el nombre de Vishnu, tranquilo y firme. Un viento levantó el chal de Holika y envolvió con él a Prahlad. Las llamas no pudieron tocarlo, y el truco de Holika no funcionó. Prahlad salió sano y salvo. Cada año, la noche antes de Holi, muchos hindúes encienden una fogata para recordarlo.

game.prompt: ¿quién hizo qué? toca las parejas.
pairs: tenía un chal que no se quemaba

es.breath: inhala despacio, tranquilo y firme como Prahlad, y exhala despacio, como el viento fresco que llevó el chal. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: puedo ser amable y seguir siendo yo

grownups.source: el Bhagavata Purana (libro 7) cuenta el amor de Prahlad por Vishnu. La fogata y Holika vienen de relatos posteriores y de Holika Dahan, la noche de la fogata antes de Holi. En algunos relatos la protección de Holika es una bendición, no un chal.
grownups.ask: ¿cuándo es difícil ser amable y seguir siendo tú?

notes: for the Keeper: Narasimha and the king's end are left out entirely, as the brief asks. Holika's fate is not described; 'her trick did not work'. Please confirm this is acceptable at Holi in families who tell the fuller story.

for the Keeper: the Bhagavata Purana does not contain the Holika episode as told at Holi; I did not cite a specific Purana for it because I am not certain which (some cite the Narada Purana or regional tellings). The wind moving the shawl is one common family version; in others Holika's boon simply fails because she used it to harm.
for the Keeper: Prahlad's line 'Vishnu is everywhere' paraphrases his teaching in Bhagavata 7 (and the pillar episode), which is otherwise omitted.

en.title: Rama comes home and the lamps are lit
en.means: the festival of lights; the name means a row of lamps

story.head: fourteen years in the forest
story.text: Prince Rama had lived in the forest for fourteen years, with his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana. Back home in the city of Ayodhya, the people missed him every single day.

story.head: sandals on the throne
story.text: Rama's brother Bharata kept Rama's place waiting for him. He set Rama's wooden sandals on the throne and cared for the kingdom in Rama's name, counting the days until his brother came back.

story.head: the flight home
story.text: At last the long trouble in Lanka was over and Sita was safe. Rama, Sita, Lakshmana and their friend Hanuman flew home together in a flying chariot called the Pushpaka, over forests and rivers.

story.head: a city full of lamps
story.text: Ayodhya ran out to meet them. Many Hindus tell that the people lit little clay lamps, called diyas, in every window and along every road, so Rama could find his way home in the dark. Families still light diyas at Diwali.

items: Bharata put Rama's sandals on the throne.
yes: he kept Rama's place and cared for the kingdom while he waited.
Rama came home riding a big gray elephant.
not in it: they flew home in a flying chariot called the Pushpaka.
the people lit lamps along every road.
yes: little clay lamps called diyas, so Rama could find his way home.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like a little lamp being lit, and breathe out slowly, like its soft glow spreading. one lamp for each breath, four in all.
en.carry: I can make someone feel welcome today

grownups.source: Valmiki's Ramayana tells of the fourteen years in the forest, Bharata and the sandals (Ayodhya Kanda), and the return to Ayodhya (end of the Yuddha Kanda). The lamps come from festival tradition. Many Hindus tell other Diwali stories too, such as Lakshmi's or Krishna's.
grownups.ask: what does it feel like when someone welcomes you home?

es.title: Rama vuelve a casa y se encienden las lámparas
es.means: la fiesta de las luces; el nombre significa hilera de lámparas

story.head: catorce años en el bosque
story.text: El príncipe Rama había vivido en el bosque catorce años, con su esposa Sita y su hermano Lakshmana. En casa, en la ciudad de Ayodhya, la gente lo extrañaba todos los días.

story.head: unas sandalias en el trono
story.text: Bharata, el hermano de Rama, le guardó su lugar. Puso las sandalias de madera de Rama en el trono y cuidó el reino en nombre de Rama, contando los días hasta que su hermano volviera.

story.head: el vuelo de regreso
story.text: Por fin terminaron los largos problemas en Lanka y Sita estaba a salvo. Rama, Sita, Lakshmana y su amigo Hanuman volvieron juntos en un carro volador llamado Pushpaka, sobre bosques y ríos.

story.head: una ciudad llena de lámparas
story.text: Ayodhya salió corriendo a recibirlos. Muchos hindúes cuentan que la gente encendió lamparitas de barro, llamadas diyas, en cada ventana y en cada camino, para que Rama encontrara el camino a casa en la oscuridad. Las familias todavía encienden diyas en Diwali.

items: Bharata puso las sandalias de Rama en el trono.
sí: le guardó su lugar y cuidó el reino mientras esperaba.
Rama volvió montado en un gran elefante gris.
no: volvieron volando en un carro volador llamado Pushpaka.
la gente encendió lámparas en cada camino.
sí: lamparitas de barro llamadas diyas, para que Rama encontrara el camino.

es.breath: inhala despacio, como una lamparita que se enciende, y exhala despacio, como su luz suave que se extiende. una lámpara por cada respiración, cuatro en total.
es.carry: puedo hacer que alguien se sienta bienvenido hoy

grownups.source: el Ramayana de Valmiki cuenta los catorce años en el bosque, Bharata y las sandalias (Ayodhya Kanda) y el regreso a Ayodhya (final del Yuddha Kanda). Las lámparas vienen de la tradición de la fiesta. Muchos hindúes cuentan también otras historias de Diwali, como la de Lakshmi o la de Krishna.
grownups.ask: ¿qué se siente cuando alguien te recibe en casa?

sources.ref: Ayodhya Kanda (the exile of fourteen years; Bharata and the sandals)
Yuddha Kanda, final sargas (the Pushpaka and the return)

notes: for the Keeper: the war with Ravana is reduced to 'the long trouble in Lanka was over'. Valmiki describes the city decorated for the return; the rows of lamps are festival tradition, so the story says 'many Hindus tell'.
for the Keeper: Hanuman travels on the Pushpaka with many companions in Valmiki; I named only Hanuman. In Valmiki, Hanuman goes ahead to tell Bharata; I left that out for length.
for the Keeper: Diwali stories vary by region (Rama in much of the north, Krishna and Narakasura in parts of the south, Lakshmi puja widely); grownups.source says so without detail.

en.title: Krishna lifts Govardhan hill
en.means: the hill Krishna lifted to shelter his village

story.head: a thank-you for the hill
story.text: In the village of Vraja, the cowherd families were getting ready a big offering for Indra, the god of rain. Young Krishna asked, “Why not thank Govardhan hill instead? It gives our cows grass and our families water.”

story.head: a great storm
story.text: So the villagers made their offering to the hill. Indra was not pleased. He sent thunder, wind and heavy rain, more and more, until the fields were flooding and the cows stood shivering.

story.head: a hill held up with one hand
story.text: Krishna walked to Govardhan and lifted the whole hill, as easily as a child picks up a mushroom. He held it high with one hand, like a giant umbrella, and called, “Come underneath, everyone, cows and calves too!”

story.head: everyone safe and dry
story.text: The whole village sheltered under the hill for seven days. Then the rain stopped. Indra understood and came to Krishna to say sorry. Many Hindus remember this with Govardhan Puja, piling up food like a little mountain.

game.prompt: who did what? tap the pairs.
pairs: lifted the hill with one hand

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like Krishna lifting the hill, and breathe out slowly, like the rain stopping at last. four slow breaths, safe and dry.
en.carry: I'll make room for someone today

grownups.source: the Bhagavata Purana, book 10 (chapters 24 to 27), tells this story. Many families say Krishna held the hill on his little finger. Govardhan Puja and Annakut, around Diwali, remember it.
grownups.ask: who is someone who shelters you when things get stormy?

es.title: Krishna levanta la colina Govardhan
es.means: la colina que Krishna levantó para proteger a su aldea

story.head: un agradecimiento para la colina
story.text: En la aldea de Vraja, las familias de pastores preparaban una gran ofrenda para Indra, el dios de la lluvia. El joven Krishna preguntó: “¿Por qué no le damos las gracias a la colina Govardhan? Les da pasto a nuestras vacas y agua a nuestras familias”.

story.head: una gran tormenta
story.text: Así que los aldeanos hicieron su ofrenda a la colina. A Indra no le gustó. Mandó truenos, viento y lluvia fuerte, más y más, hasta que los campos se inundaron y las vacas temblaban.

story.head: una colina sostenida con una mano
story.text: Krishna fue hasta Govardhan y levantó la colina entera, tan fácil como un niño levanta un hongo. La sostuvo en alto con una mano, como un paraguas gigante, y llamó: “¡Vengan todos aquí abajo, también las vacas y los terneros!”

story.head: todos a salvo y secos
story.text: Toda la aldea se refugió bajo la colina durante siete días. Luego paró la lluvia. Indra entendió y vino a pedirle perdón a Krishna. Muchos hindúes lo recuerdan con Govardhan Puja, amontonando comida como una pequeña montaña.

game.prompt: ¿quién hizo qué? toca las parejas.
pairs: levantó la colina con una mano

es.breath: inhala despacio, como Krishna levantando la colina, y exhala despacio, como la lluvia que por fin para. cuatro respiraciones lentas, a salvo y secos.
es.carry: hoy le haré un lugar a alguien

grownups.source: el Bhagavata Purana, libro 10 (capítulos 24 a 27), cuenta esta historia. Muchas familias dicen que Krishna sostuvo la colina con el dedo meñique. Govardhan Puja y Annakut, cerca de Diwali, la recuerdan.
grownups.ask: ¿quién te protege cuando las cosas se ponen difíciles?

notes: for the Keeper: the Bhagavata says Krishna lifted the hill with one hand 'as a child holds a mushroom' and held it for seven days; the little finger is the popular image, mentioned in grownups.source. Please confirm the seven days (I recall 10.25.23).

for the Keeper: Krishna's age and his exact argument (honor the hill, the cows and the brahmins) are simplified. Govardhan Puja/Annakut falls the day after Diwali in much of north India; I wrote 'around Diwali'.

en.title: Dhruva and the pole star
en.means: the name means steady; the star that stays in its place

story.head: no room on the king's lap
story.text: Little Prince Dhruva ran to sit on his father's lap. But the king's other wife, Suruchi, said there was no room for him there. Dhruva walked away with tears on his cheeks.

story.head: his mother's advice
story.text: His mother, Suniti, hugged him close. “Don't be angry,” she said softly. “Turn to Vishnu. He welcomes everyone.” So Dhruva set off for the forest, small and very brave.

story.head: Narada the wandering sage
story.text: On the way he met Narada, a wandering sage who carries a veena. Narada saw how determined the boy was, and taught him how to sit very still and think of Vishnu with a quiet heart.

story.head: a star that never moves
story.text: Dhruva sat so still, for so long, that Vishnu came to him. Dhruva's sadness melted away. Vishnu gave him a place in the sky that would never move: the pole star, steady all night, still showing travelers the way north.

items: Dhruva's mother told him to turn to Vishnu.
yes: Suniti hugged him and said Vishnu welcomes everyone.
Dhruva became the moon.
not in it: he became the pole star, the star that stays in its place.
Narada met Dhruva on his way to the forest.
yes: the wandering sage taught him to sit still and think of Vishnu.

en.breath: breathe in slowly and breathe out slowly, steady as the pole star. four slow breaths, still and bright in a dark sky.
en.carry: I'll find room for someone who feels left out

grownups.source: the Bhagavata Purana (book 4, chapters 8 and 9) and the Vishnu Purana (book 1) tell Dhruva's story. In the texts Dhruva goes home afterward and rules for a long time before taking his place in the sky.
grownups.ask: what helps you feel better when you feel left out?

es.title: Dhruva y la estrella polar
es.means: el nombre significa firme; la estrella que no se mueve

story.head: no hay lugar en las piernas del rey
story.text: El pequeño príncipe Dhruva corrió a sentarse en las piernas de su papá. Pero la otra esposa del rey, Suruchi, le dijo que ahí no había lugar para él. Dhruva se fue con lágrimas en las mejillas.

story.head: el consejo de su mamá
story.text: Su mamá, Suniti, lo abrazó fuerte. “No te enojes”, le dijo con dulzura. “Busca a Vishnu. Él recibe a todos”. Así que Dhruva se fue al bosque, pequeño y muy valiente.

story.head: Narada, el sabio viajero
story.text: En el camino se encontró con Narada, un sabio viajero que lleva una vina. Narada vio lo decidido que estaba el niño y le enseñó a sentarse muy quieto y pensar en Vishnu con el corazón tranquilo.

story.head: una estrella que nunca se mueve
story.text: Dhruva se quedó tan quieto, por tanto tiempo, que Vishnu vino a verlo. La tristeza de Dhruva se deshizo. Vishnu le dio un lugar en el cielo que nunca se movería: la estrella polar, firme toda la noche, que todavía les muestra el norte a los viajeros.

items: la mamá de Dhruva le dijo que buscara a Vishnu.
sí: Suniti lo abrazó y le dijo que Vishnu recibe a todos.
Dhruva se convirtió en la luna.
no: se convirtió en la estrella polar, la estrella que no se mueve.
Narada se encontró con Dhruva camino al bosque.
sí: el sabio viajero le enseñó a quedarse quieto y pensar en Vishnu.

es.breath: inhala despacio y exhala despacio, firme como la estrella polar. cuatro respiraciones lentas, quietas y brillantes en el cielo oscuro.
es.carry: le haré lugar a alguien que se siente excluido

grownups.source: el Bhagavata Purana (libro 4, capítulos 8 y 9) y el Vishnu Purana (libro 1) cuentan la historia de Dhruva. En los textos, Dhruva vuelve a casa y reina mucho tiempo antes de ocupar su lugar en el cielo.
grownups.ask: ¿qué te ayuda a sentirte mejor cuando te sientes excluido?

notes: for the Keeper: Suruchi is not called unkind; she only says there is no room. The Bhagavata gives Dhruva's age (five) and his austerities in detail; both left out. Narada gives him a mantra (om namo bhagavate vasudevaya), which I did not name; a Keeper may want it named.
for the Keeper: Vishnu Purana chapter numbers (1.11-12) are from memory; please check.

en.title: baby Krishna and the butter
en.means: a name of Krishna: the one with a rope around his tummy

story.head: Yashoda churns the butter
story.text: In the village of Gokul, Krishna's mother Yashoda was churning milk into butter, singing about her little boy as she worked. Baby Krishna toddled over, hungry, and climbed into her lap for his milk.

story.head: a broken pot of yogurt
story.text: When the milk on the stove started to boil over, Yashoda hurried away. Krishna pouted. He cracked a clay pot of yogurt with a stone and slipped off to eat fresh butter. He shared it with the monkeys too!

story.head: a rope too short
story.text: Yashoda came back, frowning and smiling at the same time. She decided to tie him to a big wooden mortar. But the rope was two fingers too short. She added more rope. Still two fingers too short!

story.head: only love can tie Krishna
story.text: Yashoda tried and tried until she was hot and tired. When Krishna saw his mother so tired, he let the rope go around him at last. The story says nothing can hold Krishna except love.

game.prompt: who did what? tap the pairs.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like the churning going round, and breathe out slowly, like soft butter rising to the top. four slow, gentle breaths.
en.carry: I'll share a treat with someone today

grownups.source: the Bhagavata Purana, book 10, chapter 9, tells how Yashoda tried to tie little Krishna and the rope was always too short. His name Damodara comes from this story, and many Vaishnava families remember it in the month of Kartik.
grownups.ask: why do you think only love could tie Krishna?

es.title: el bebé Krishna y la mantequilla
es.means: un nombre de Krishna: el que tiene una cuerda en la pancita

story.head: Yashoda bate la mantequilla
story.text: En la aldea de Gokul, Yashoda, la mamá de Krishna, batía leche para hacer mantequilla y cantaba sobre su niño mientras trabajaba. El bebé Krishna llegó caminando, con hambre, y se subió a su regazo a tomar leche.

story.head: una olla de yogur rota
story.text: Cuando la leche en el fuego empezó a derramarse, Yashoda salió corriendo. Krishna hizo pucheros. Rompió una olla de barro con yogur usando una piedra y se escapó a comer mantequilla fresca. ¡También la compartió con los monos!

story.head: una cuerda demasiado corta
story.text: Yashoda volvió, enojada y sonriente a la vez. Decidió atarlo a un gran mortero de madera. Pero a la cuerda le faltaban dos dedos. Le agregó más cuerda. ¡Otra vez le faltaban dos dedos!

story.head: solo el amor puede atar a Krishna
story.text: Yashoda lo intentó una y otra vez hasta quedar acalorada y cansada. Cuando Krishna vio a su mamá tan cansada, por fin dejó que la cuerda lo rodeara. La historia dice que nada puede sujetar a Krishna, excepto el amor.

game.prompt: ¿quién hizo qué? toca las parejas.

es.breath: inhala despacio, como la leche que da vueltas al batirla, y exhala despacio, como la mantequilla suave que sube. cuatro respiraciones lentas y suaves.
es.carry: hoy compartiré algo rico con alguien

grownups.source: el Bhagavata Purana, libro 10, capítulo 9, cuenta cómo Yashoda intentó atar al pequeño Krishna y la cuerda siempre era corta. De esta historia viene su nombre Damodara, y muchas familias vaishnavas la recuerdan en el mes de Kartik.
grownups.ask: ¿por qué crees que solo el amor podía atar a Krishna?

notes: for the Keeper: being tied to the mortar is the heart of the text; I kept it light (no tears, no stick). In the Bhagavata Yashoda picks up a stick and Krishna cries in fear; both left out. Please confirm the tying itself is acceptable for small children.

for the Keeper: 'nothing can hold Krishna except love' paraphrases the chapter's teaching that the Lord is bound only by devotion (bhakti); it is not a quotation. The Kartik remembrance (Damodara month) belongs to some Vaishnava communities, hence 'many Vaishnava families'.

en.title: Yashoda looks inside Krishna's mouth
en.means: Krishna's mother, who raised him in the village of Gokul

story.head: a report about mud
story.text: One day Krishna's brother Balarama and their friends came running to Yashoda. “Krishna ate mud!” they told her. Yashoda put her hands on her hips and looked at her little son.

story.head: open your mouth
story.text: “Did you eat mud?” she asked. “No, Mother,” said Krishna. “They're just teasing. Look for yourself.” And he opened his mouth wide, wide, wide.

story.head: the whole universe inside
story.text: Yashoda peered in and gasped. Inside she saw the sky and the stars, the sun and the moon, mountains, oceans and islands. She saw the whole universe, and even her own village, and herself, looking in!

story.head: a hug and a forgetting
story.text: Yashoda stood amazed. Then, the story says, Krishna gently let her forget what she had seen, so she could simply be his mother again. She scooped him up, laughing, and hugged him close.

items: Krishna's friends said he had eaten mud.
yes: Balarama and the friends came running to tell Yashoda.
Yashoda saw stars and oceans inside his mouth.
yes: she saw the whole universe, even her village and herself.
Yashoda sent Krishna to bed without supper.
not in it: she forgot what she saw and hugged him close.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, as wide as the sky Yashoda saw, and breathe out slowly, as soft as her hug. four slow breaths.
en.carry: I'll look for something amazing in an ordinary day

grownups.source: the Bhagavata Purana, book 10, chapter 8, tells this story. In the text Krishna lets Yashoda forget through his maya, his power of wonder, so her love as a mother can go on.
grownups.ask: if you could look inside something small and see something huge, what would you hope to see?

es.title: Yashoda mira dentro de la boca de Krishna
es.means: la mamá de Krishna, que lo crio en la aldea de Gokul

story.head: una noticia sobre el lodo
story.text: Un día, Balarama, el hermano de Krishna, y sus amigos llegaron corriendo a ver a Yashoda. “¡Krishna comió lodo!”, le dijeron. Yashoda se puso las manos en la cintura y miró a su hijito.

story.head: abre la boca
story.text: “¿Comiste lodo?”, le preguntó. “No, mamá”, dijo Krishna. “Solo me están molestando. Mira tú misma”. Y abrió la boca grande, grande, grande.

story.head: todo el universo adentro
story.text: Yashoda se asomó y se quedó sin aliento. Adentro vio el cielo y las estrellas, el sol y la luna, montañas, mares e islas. Vio todo el universo, ¡y hasta su propia aldea, y a ella misma, mirando!

story.head: un abrazo y un olvido
story.text: Yashoda se quedó asombrada. Entonces, dice la historia, Krishna dejó con suavidad que olvidara lo que había visto, para que pudiera ser simplemente su mamá otra vez. Ella lo levantó riendo y lo abrazó fuerte.

items: los amigos de Krishna dijeron que había comido lodo.
sí: Balarama y los amigos llegaron corriendo a contarle a Yashoda.
Yashoda vio estrellas y mares dentro de su boca.
sí: vio todo el universo, hasta su aldea y a ella misma.
Yashoda mandó a Krishna a la cama sin cenar.
no: olvidó lo que vio y lo abrazó fuerte.

es.breath: inhala despacio, tan amplio como el cielo que vio Yashoda, y exhala despacio, tan suave como su abrazo. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: buscaré algo asombroso en un día normal

grownups.source: el Bhagavata Purana, libro 10, capítulo 8, cuenta esta historia. En el texto, Krishna deja que Yashoda olvide por medio de su maya, su poder de asombro, para que su amor de madre pueda seguir.
grownups.ask: si pudieras mirar dentro de algo pequeño y ver algo enorme, ¿qué te gustaría ver?

sources.ref: book 10, chapter 8 (the universe in Krishna's mouth)

notes: for the Keeper: 'They're just teasing' softens Krishna's words in the text (he says they are lying). 'Maya, his power of wonder' is a child-sized gloss of Vaishnava maya / yogamaya; please confirm the wording.
for the Keeper: in the text Yashoda reasons through who her son is before the forgetting; condensed here.

en.title: Sudama's handful of rice
en.means: Krishna's childhood friend, poor in money and rich in love

story.head: two friends at school
story.text: When they were boys, Krishna and Sudama studied together with the same teacher, sharing chores and jokes. Years later, Krishna lived in a palace in Dwaraka, and Sudama lived in a tiny hut with hardly any food.

story.head: a gift tied in a cloth
story.text: Sudama's wife said, “Go and visit your old friend.” But what gift could he bring? She found a little flattened rice, and Sudama tied it up in a corner of his old cloth.

story.head: Krishna runs to hug him
story.text: When Krishna saw Sudama at the door, he jumped up and hugged him. He washed his friend's tired feet and gave him his own seat. Sudama felt too shy to show his little gift.

story.head: the handful of rice
story.text: Krishna found the bundle and laughed with delight. He ate a handful of the rice as if it were a feast. Sudama walked home without asking for anything, and found his hut had become a fine house, full of good things.

game.prompt: who did what? tap the pairs.
pairs: ate it as if it were a feast

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like a hug from an old friend, and breathe out slowly, like the long walk home. four slow breaths.
en.carry: I'll give a small gift from the heart today

grownups.source: the Bhagavata Purana, book 10, chapters 80 and 81. The text calls him a brahmin friend of Krishna; the name Sudama comes from later tellings, and in South India many know him as Kuchela.
grownups.ask: what small gift could you give a friend that would mean a lot?

es.title: el puñado de arroz de Sudama
es.means: el amigo de infancia de Krishna, pobre en dinero y rico en amor

story.head: dos amigos en la escuela
story.text: Cuando eran niños, Krishna y Sudama estudiaban juntos con el mismo maestro, compartiendo tareas y bromas. Años después, Krishna vivía en un palacio en Dwaraka, y Sudama vivía en una choza pequeñita, casi sin comida.

story.head: un regalo atado en un paño
story.text: La esposa de Sudama le dijo: “Ve a visitar a tu viejo amigo”. Pero ¿qué regalo podía llevar? Ella encontró un poco de arroz aplastado, y Sudama lo ató en una esquina de su paño viejo.

story.head: Krishna corre a abrazarlo
story.text: Cuando Krishna vio a Sudama en la puerta, se levantó de un salto y lo abrazó. Le lavó los pies cansados a su amigo y le dio su propio asiento. Sudama sentía demasiada vergüenza para mostrar su regalito.

story.head: el puñado de arroz
story.text: Krishna encontró el paquetito y se rio de alegría. Se comió un puñado de arroz como si fuera un banquete. Sudama volvió a casa sin pedir nada, y encontró que su choza se había vuelto una casa hermosa, llena de cosas buenas.

game.prompt: ¿quién hizo qué? toca las parejas.
pairs: llevó un poco de arroz aplastado

es.breath: inhala despacio, como el abrazo de un viejo amigo, y exhala despacio, como el largo camino a casa. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: hoy daré un regalito de corazón

grownups.source: el Bhagavata Purana, libro 10, capítulos 80 y 81. El texto lo llama un amigo brahmán de Krishna; el nombre Sudama viene de relatos posteriores, y en el sur de la India muchos lo conocen como Kuchela.
grownups.ask: ¿qué regalito podrías darle a un amigo que significaría mucho?

notes: for the Keeper: in the text the wife begs the rice from neighbors (a set number of handfuls); simplified to 'found a little flattened rice'. Rukmini stops Krishna after the first handful; left out.
for the Keeper: the teacher (Sandipani) is unnamed here. Please confirm the Kuchela note for South Indian families.

en.title: Shabari's berries
en.means: a woman of the forest who waited years to welcome Rama

story.head: Shabari waits by the path
story.text: Deep in the forest lived an old woman named Shabari. Her teachers had told her that one day Prince Rama would come by. So every morning she swept the path clean and waited.

story.head: picking the sweetest berries
story.text: Every day she picked wild berries for Rama. She tasted each one and kept only the sweetest, so Rama would get nothing sour. Days became years. Shabari's hair turned white, and still she waited.

story.head: Rama comes at last
story.text: One day Rama and his brother Lakshmana really did come walking down the path. Shabari's heart leaped. She washed their feet, gave them a place to sit, and offered her basket of tasted berries.

story.head: the sweetest gift
story.text: Rama ate every berry with a smile. He didn't mind at all that she had tasted them first. In the story, what Rama saw was her love, and that mattered more to him than any fruit.

items: Shabari tasted each berry to keep the sweetest.
yes: she kept only the sweet ones, so Rama would get nothing sour.
Rama said the berries were too sour to eat.
not in it: he ate every berry with a smile and saw only her love.
Shabari swept the path while she waited.
yes: every morning she swept the path clean and waited for Rama.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like Shabari waiting by the path, and breathe out slowly, like her smile when Rama came. four slow breaths.
en.carry: I'll give my best to someone today

grownups.source: Valmiki's Ramayana (near the end of the Aranya Kanda) tells of Shabari welcoming Rama with forest fruits. The tasted berries come from later devotional tellings and family storytelling.
grownups.ask: what is something you made or picked especially for someone you love?

es.title: las moras de Shabari
es.means: una mujer del bosque que esperó años para recibir a Rama

story.head: Shabari espera junto al camino
story.text: En lo profundo del bosque vivía una anciana llamada Shabari. Sus maestros le habían dicho que algún día el príncipe Rama pasaría por ahí. Así que cada mañana barría el camino y esperaba.

story.head: las moras más dulces
story.text: Cada día recogía moras silvestres para Rama. Probaba cada una y guardaba solo las más dulces, para que a Rama no le tocara ninguna agria. Los días se volvieron años. El cabello de Shabari se puso blanco, y ella seguía esperando.

story.head: por fin llega Rama
story.text: Un día, Rama y su hermano Lakshmana de verdad llegaron caminando por el sendero. El corazón de Shabari dio un salto. Les lavó los pies, les dio dónde sentarse y les ofreció su canasta de moras probadas.

story.head: el regalo más dulce
story.text: Rama se comió cada mora con una sonrisa. No le importó nada que ella las hubiera probado primero. En la historia, lo que Rama vio fue su amor, y eso le importaba más que cualquier fruta.

items: Shabari probaba cada mora para guardar las más dulces.
sí: guardaba solo las dulces, para que a Rama no le tocara ninguna agria.
Rama dijo que las moras estaban muy agrias.
no: se comió cada mora con una sonrisa y solo vio su amor.
Shabari barría el camino mientras esperaba.
sí: cada mañana barría el camino y esperaba a Rama.

es.breath: inhala despacio, como Shabari esperando junto al camino, y exhala despacio, como su sonrisa cuando llegó Rama. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: hoy le daré lo mejor de mí a alguien

grownups.source: el Ramayana de Valmiki (cerca del final del Aranya Kanda) cuenta cómo Shabari recibió a Rama con frutas del bosque. Las moras probadas vienen de relatos devocionales posteriores y de las familias.
grownups.ask: ¿qué hiciste o escogiste especialmente para alguien que quieres?

notes: for the Keeper: Valmiki has Shabari offer fruits and then leave her body; her passing is left out. The tasted berries (ber, jujube) are from later bhakti tellings; I did not attribute them to a named poet because I am not certain which text first has them.
for the Keeper: 'berries' / 'moras' stands for ber (Indian jujube); Spanish 'moras' is a loose rendering. A Keeper may prefer 'frutas' or 'ber'.

en.title: the squirrel who helped build the bridge
en.means: helping others with love, without asking for anything back

story.head: a bridge across the sea
story.text: Rama needed to cross the sea to bring Sita home. So the monkey army began to build a bridge, carrying huge rocks and whole trees and dropping them into the waves, splash after splash.

story.head: a tiny helper
story.text: On the beach, a little squirrel watched. “I want to help too,” she thought. She rolled in the sand, ran onto the bridge, and shook the sand off into the cracks between the rocks. Then back she ran for more.

story.head: a monkey laughs
story.text: A big monkey laughed. “Little one, what good is a bit of sand?” But the squirrel kept going, back and forth, all day long, filling every gap she could find.

story.head: stripes from Rama's fingers
story.text: Rama saw her. He picked her up gently and stroked her back with his fingers. “Every bit of help counts,” he said. Many families say that is why the little squirrels of India have stripes on their backs.

game.prompt: who did what? tap the pairs.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like the squirrel rolling in the sand, and breathe out slowly, like the sand falling into place. four slow breaths.
en.carry: I'll do one small helpful thing today

grownups.source: Valmiki's Ramayana (Yuddha Kanda) tells of the bridge built by Nala and the monkey army. The squirrel is not in Valmiki; it comes from later tellings in several Indian languages and from family storytelling.
grownups.ask: what is a small way you helped today that someone might not have noticed?

es.title: la ardilla que ayudó a construir el puente
es.means: ayudar a otros con amor, sin pedir nada a cambio

story.head: un puente sobre el mar
story.text: Rama necesitaba cruzar el mar para traer a Sita a casa. Así que el ejército de monos empezó a construir un puente, cargando rocas enormes y árboles enteros y dejándolos caer en las olas, ¡plaf, plaf!

story.head: una ayudante pequeñita
story.text: En la playa, una ardillita miraba. “Yo también quiero ayudar”, pensó. Se revolcó en la arena, corrió al puente y se sacudió la arena en las grietas entre las rocas. Luego volvió corriendo por más.

story.head: un mono se ríe
story.text: Un mono grande se rio. “Pequeña, ¿de qué sirve un poquito de arena?”. Pero la ardilla siguió, de ida y de vuelta, todo el día, llenando cada hueco que encontraba.

story.head: rayas de los dedos de Rama
story.text: Rama la vio. La levantó con cuidado y le acarició la espalda con los dedos. “Toda ayuda cuenta”, dijo. Muchas familias dicen que por eso las ardillitas de la India tienen rayas en la espalda.

game.prompt: ¿quién hizo qué? toca las parejas.

es.breath: inhala despacio, como la ardilla revolcándose en la arena, y exhala despacio, como la arena cayendo en su lugar. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: hoy haré una pequeña cosa para ayudar

grownups.source: el Ramayana de Valmiki (Yuddha Kanda) cuenta cómo Nala y el ejército de monos construyeron el puente. La ardilla no está en Valmiki; viene de relatos posteriores en varias lenguas de la India y de las familias.
grownups.ask: ¿de qué manera pequeña ayudaste hoy sin que nadie lo notara?

sources.ref: Yuddha Kanda (Nala builds the bridge, Setu)

notes: for the Keeper: the squirrel's source is uncertain; it is widely told in South India and sometimes credited to regional Ramayanas, but I could not confirm a specific text, so I wrote 'later tellings in several Indian languages'. The usual telling says three stripes from three fingers; I gave no count.
for the Keeper: the laughing monkey is kept mild; some tellings have Rama gently correct the monkeys. Rama's line is a paraphrase of the usual family telling.

en.title: Ganesha writes the Mahabharata
en.means: a very long Hindu epic, the great story of the Bharata family

story.head: a story too big to write alone
story.text: The sage Vyasa had a huge story in his mind: the Mahabharata, full of heroes, families, battles of the heart and wise words. It was so long that he needed someone very fast to write it down as he spoke.

story.head: Ganesha's one rule
story.text: Ganesha, the god of wisdom, said yes, with one rule: “Once I start writing, you must not stop speaking.” Vyasa smiled and added a rule of his own: “Then you must understand every verse before you write it.”

story.head: a pen breaks
story.text: So they began. Vyasa spoke and Ganesha wrote. Whenever Vyasa needed a moment to think, he said a tricky verse, and Ganesha paused to work it out. One day, many tell, Ganesha's pen broke!

story.head: a tusk for a pen
story.text: Ganesha did not stop. He snapped off the tip of one of his own tusks and kept writing with it. That is why, in many pictures, Ganesha has one whole tusk and one broken one.

items: Ganesha said Vyasa must not stop speaking.
yes: that was Ganesha's rule, and Vyasa added one of his own.
Vyasa wrote the whole story down himself.
not in it: Vyasa spoke, and Ganesha did the writing.
Ganesha used his broken tusk as a pen.
yes: when his pen broke, he kept writing with his tusk.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like Vyasa thinking of the next verse, and breathe out slowly, like Ganesha's pen moving across the page. four slow breaths.
en.carry: I'll finish something I started

grownups.source: the opening of the Mahabharata (Adi Parva) in many printed versions tells of Ganesha as Vyasa's scribe; some scholarly editions leave this passage out. The broken tusk as a pen comes from later tellings.
grownups.ask: what would you want to write down so it's never forgotten?

es.title: Ganesha escribe el Mahabharata
es.means: un poema épico hindú muy largo, la gran historia de la familia Bharata

story.head: una historia muy grande
story.text: El sabio Vyasa tenía en la mente una historia enorme: el Mahabharata, lleno de héroes, familias, luchas del corazón y palabras sabias. Era tan larga que necesitaba a alguien muy rápido que la escribiera mientras él hablaba.

story.head: la regla de Ganesha
story.text: Ganesha, el dios de la sabiduría, dijo que sí, con una regla: “Una vez que empiece a escribir, no puedes dejar de hablar”. Vyasa sonrió y puso una regla propia: “Entonces debes entender cada verso antes de escribirlo”.

story.head: se rompe la pluma
story.text: Así empezaron. Vyasa hablaba y Ganesha escribía. Cuando Vyasa necesitaba un momento para pensar, decía un verso difícil, y Ganesha se detenía a descifrarlo. Un día, cuentan muchos, ¡la pluma de Ganesha se rompió!

story.head: un colmillo como pluma
story.text: Ganesha no se detuvo. Se quitó la punta de uno de sus colmillos y siguió escribiendo con ella. Por eso, en muchas imágenes, Ganesha tiene un colmillo entero y uno roto.

items: Ganesha dijo que Vyasa no podía dejar de hablar.
sí: esa era la regla de Ganesha, y Vyasa puso una propia.
Vyasa escribió él mismo toda la historia.
no: Vyasa hablaba y Ganesha escribía.
Ganesha usó su colmillo roto como pluma.
sí: cuando se le rompió la pluma, siguió escribiendo con su colmillo.

es.breath: inhala despacio, como Vyasa pensando el siguiente verso, y exhala despacio, como la pluma de Ganesha moviéndose por la página. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: terminaré algo que empecé

grownups.source: el comienzo del Mahabharata (Adi Parva), en muchas ediciones impresas, cuenta que Ganesha fue el escriba de Vyasa; algunas ediciones académicas omiten este pasaje. El colmillo roto como pluma viene de relatos posteriores.
grownups.ask: ¿qué te gustaría escribir para que nunca se olvide?

sources.ref: Adi Parva, chapter 1 (Ganesha as scribe; vulgate versions)

notes: for the Keeper: the Ganesha-as-scribe passage is in the vulgate (e.g. Ganguli's source text) but relegated from the Pune critical edition; grownups.source says so plainly. The broken tusk as pen is a popular telling; other Puranic stories explain the broken tusk differently (e.g. a fight with Parashurama). Not mentioned to keep it gentle.
for the Keeper: 'battles of the heart' is used to avoid describing the Kurukshetra war.

en.title: baby Hanuman and the sun
en.means: the sun, and the god of the sun

story.head: a big orange fruit
story.text: When Hanuman was a baby, he woke up very hungry. He looked out and saw the rising sun, round and orange and glowing. “What a delicious fruit!” he thought, and his tummy rumbled.

story.head: a leap toward the sun
story.text: Baby Hanuman, son of Vayu the wind, jumped up into the sky, higher and higher, reaching for the sun with his little hands. The gods in the sky could hardly believe their eyes.

story.head: a bump on the chin
story.text: Indra, king of the gods, stopped the baby before he reached the sun. Hanuman tumbled back down to earth and bumped his chin. Some say that is how he got his name, from hanu, an old word for jaw.

story.head: blessings for Hanuman
story.text: Vayu the wind was so sad that he stopped blowing, and everything grew still. So the gods came, comforted Vayu, helped Hanuman feel well again, and each gave the baby a blessing. The wind blew again, and Hanuman grew up strong and wise.

game.prompt: who did what? tap the pairs.
pairs: thought the sun was a fruit
stopped the wind for a while

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like the wind filling the sky, and breathe out slowly, like the wind blowing gently again. four slow breaths.
en.carry: I'll comfort someone who feels sad

grownups.source: Valmiki's Ramayana tells it twice: Jambavan recalls it near the end of the Kishkindha Kanda, and the Uttara Kanda tells it again. In the text Indra strikes with his thunderbolt; families tell it gently, as here.
grownups.ask: what is something you wanted so much you reached for it like baby Hanuman?

es.title: el bebé Hanuman y el sol
es.means: el sol, y el dios del sol

story.head: una gran fruta anaranjada
story.text: Cuando Hanuman era bebé, se despertó con mucha hambre. Miró afuera y vio el sol que salía, redondo, anaranjado y brillante. “¡Qué fruta tan rica!”, pensó, y le sonó la pancita.

story.head: un salto hacia el sol
story.text: El bebé Hanuman, hijo de Vayu, el viento, saltó al cielo, cada vez más alto, estirando sus manitas hacia el sol. Los dioses del cielo casi no podían creer lo que veían.

story.head: un golpecito en la barbilla
story.text: Indra, el rey de los dioses, detuvo al bebé antes de que llegara al sol. Hanuman cayó rodando a la tierra y se golpeó la barbilla. Algunos dicen que de ahí viene su nombre, de hanu, una palabra antigua para mandíbula.

story.head: bendiciones para Hanuman
story.text: Vayu, el viento, se puso tan triste que dejó de soplar, y todo se quedó quieto. Entonces vinieron los dioses, consolaron a Vayu, ayudaron a Hanuman a sentirse bien otra vez, y cada uno le dio una bendición al bebé. El viento volvió a soplar, y Hanuman creció fuerte y sabio.

game.prompt: ¿quién hizo qué? toca las parejas.
pairs: creyó que el sol era una fruta

es.breath: inhala despacio, como el viento que llena el cielo, y exhala despacio, como el viento que vuelve a soplar suave. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: consolaré a alguien que esté triste

grownups.source: el Ramayana de Valmiki lo cuenta dos veces: Jambavan lo recuerda cerca del final del Kishkindha Kanda, y el Uttara Kanda lo vuelve a contar. En el texto Indra lo golpea con su rayo; las familias lo cuentan con suavidad, como aquí.
grownups.ask: ¿qué has querido tanto que lo buscaste como el bebé Hanuman?

sources.ref: Kishkindha Kanda, final sargas (Jambavan's account); Uttara Kanda (Hanuman's childhood)

notes: for the Keeper: the thunderbolt (vajra) striking Hanuman is softened to 'stopped' and 'bumped his chin'; in some tellings Hanuman is struck lifeless and revived by Brahma. Please confirm the softening.
for the Keeper: the hanu (jaw) etymology is given in the Ramayana itself, I believe in the Kishkindha Kanda account; I wrote 'some say' to be safe. Exact sarga numbers not cited.
for the Keeper: the later telling that Surya became Hanuman's teacher is left out; the word Surya is introduced because the sun is central to the story.

en.title: Ganga comes down through Shiva's hair
en.means: गंगा: the river Ganges, honored by many Hindus as a goddess

story.head: a river in the sky
story.text: Long ago, the story says, the river Ganga flowed only in the heavens. On earth, a king named Bhagiratha wished she would come down, so her water could bring peace to his ancestors, who had died long before.

story.head: Bhagiratha's long prayer
story.text: Bhagiratha prayed for a long, long time. At last Ganga agreed to come. But she was so strong and so fast that if she fell straight onto the earth, the ground would crack.

story.head: caught in Shiva's hair
story.text: So Bhagiratha asked Shiva for help. Shiva stood on the mountain and let the mighty river fall onto his head. Ganga tumbled into his long, tangled hair and wandered around and around inside it.

story.head: Ganga flows gently down
story.text: Then Shiva let her out gently, a little at a time. Ganga flowed down from the mountains and across the land, following Bhagiratha, who led the way, all the way to the sea.

items: Shiva caught Ganga in his long hair.
yes: she tumbled into his tangled hair and came out gently.
Bhagiratha asked the ocean to carry Ganga.
not in it: he asked Shiva to catch her as she fell.
Ganga followed Bhagiratha across the land.
yes: he led the way, and she flowed all the way to the sea.

en.breath: breathe in slowly, like the river falling softly into Shiva's hair, and breathe out slowly, like it flowing gently to the sea. four slow breaths.
en.carry: when I have big feelings, I'll let them out gently

grownups.source: Valmiki's Ramayana (Bala Kanda) and the Bhagavata Purana (book 9) tell how Bhagiratha brought Ganga to earth. In Hindi a huge, patient effort is still called a Bhagirath prayas, a Bhagiratha effort.
grownups.ask: when have you had to be gentle with something strong, like a big feeling?

es.title: Ganga baja por el cabello de Shiva
es.means: गंगा: el río Ganges, honrado por muchos hindúes como diosa

story.head: un río en el cielo
story.text: Hace mucho tiempo, dice la historia, el río Ganga corría solo en los cielos. En la tierra, un rey llamado Bhagiratha deseaba que bajara, para que su agua diera paz a sus antepasados, que habían muerto mucho tiempo atrás.

story.head: la larga oración de Bhagiratha
story.text: Bhagiratha oró durante mucho, mucho tiempo. Por fin Ganga aceptó venir. Pero era tan fuerte y tan rápida que, si caía de golpe sobre la tierra, el suelo se partiría.

story.head: atrapada en el cabello de Shiva
story.text: Entonces Bhagiratha le pidió ayuda a Shiva. Shiva se paró en la montaña y dejó que el gran río le cayera sobre la cabeza. Ganga cayó en su cabello largo y enredado, y dio vueltas y vueltas adentro.

story.head: Ganga baja con suavidad
story.text: Después Shiva la dejó salir con suavidad, poco a poco. Ganga bajó de las montañas y cruzó la tierra, siguiendo a Bhagiratha, que iba adelante, hasta llegar al mar.

items: Shiva atrapó a Ganga en su cabello largo.
sí: cayó en su cabello enredado y salió con suavidad.
Bhagiratha le pidió al océano que llevara a Ganga.
no: le pidió a Shiva que la atrapara al caer.
Ganga siguió a Bhagiratha por la tierra.
sí: él iba adelante, y ella corrió hasta el mar.

es.breath: inhala despacio, como el río que cae suave en el cabello de Shiva, y exhala despacio, como el agua que corre tranquila hasta el mar. cuatro respiraciones lentas.
es.carry: cuando sienta algo muy fuerte, lo dejaré salir con calma

grownups.source: el Ramayana de Valmiki (Bala Kanda) y el Bhagavata Purana (libro 9) cuentan cómo Bhagiratha trajo a Ganga a la tierra. En hindi, un esfuerzo enorme y paciente todavía se llama Bhagirath prayas, un esfuerzo de Bhagiratha.
grownups.ask: ¿cuándo tuviste que tratar con suavidad algo muy fuerte, como un sentimiento grande?

sources.ref: Bala Kanda, sargas 38 to 44 (Sagara and Bhagiratha)

notes: for the Keeper: Sagara's sons being burned to ashes by the sage Kapila is reduced to 'his ancestors, who had died long before'. Strictly they are Bhagiratha's great-great-granduncles; 'ancestors' avoids the count. Sarga numbers (38-44) and Bhagavata 9.9 are from memory; please check.
for the Keeper: Ganga's pride (wanting to sweep Shiva away) and the sage Jahnu drinking her are left out for length.

en.title: Arjuna and the bird's eye
en.means: a teacher, like Drona, who taught the young princes

story.head: a wooden bird in a tree
story.text: The teacher Drona taught archery to the young princes. One day he set a wooden bird high up in a tree. “Today's test,” he said, “is to hit the bird's eye.”

story.head: what do you see?
story.text: He called the eldest prince, Yudhishthira. “Aim, and tell me what you see.” Yudhishthira said, “I see the tree, the bird, you, and my brothers.” Drona said kindly, “Put down your bow.”

story.head: everyone sees too much
story.text: One by one, the other princes tried. Each one saw the leaves, the sky, the tree, the people watching. Drona asked each of them to step aside.

story.head: Arjuna sees only the eye
story.text: Then came Arjuna. “What do you see?” asked Drona. “Only the bird's eye,” said Arjuna. “Shoot,” said Drona. Arjuna's arrow flew straight to the mark. He had given his whole attention to one thing.
